newsitem.title: JAPAN: Surging imports help keep Japan surplus shrinking.
newsitem.headline: Surging imports help keep Japan surplus shrinking.

text.p: Surging imports and large outflows of yen into foreign investment helped keep Japan's trade and current account surpluses shrinking in August.

The surplus in the current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services and often a source of contention with the United States and other trading partners, fell by 28.9 percent in August from a year earlier to 460.60 billion yen ($4.14 billion), the Finance Ministry said on Wednesday.
The surplus in merchandise trade alone fell by 27.8 percent to 566.70 billion yen ($5.10 billion) from August last year.
But economists said the pace of the drop in the surplus, which has been on a declining trend for a year, had slowed and would decelerate more as exports picked up due to a weaker yen.
A weak yen makes Japanese products more competitive in overseas markets because it enables Japanese firms to cut prices of their products abroad.
"The current account surplus is on a declining trend with the increase in imports outpacing increases in exports," a senior ministry official told reporters.
The official said a huge increase in outflows of Japanese money to overseas markets was a major reason for the drop in the overall current account surplus in August.
The balance of payments in securities investment showed a deficit of 1.08 trillion yen ($9.75 billion), compared with a deficit of 72.2 billion yen ($650 million) a year earlier.

"On the capital flow account, we do see some evidence of Japanese appetite for international securities... The focus now falls entirely on capital flows with the record low interest rates in Japan compared with higher interest rates in the U.S. and elsewhere," Jesper Koll, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Tokyo, told Reuters Financial Television.
Japan's interest rates have been kept at record low levels since September last year when the Bank of Japan, the nation's central bank, cut its official discount rate to 0.5 percent.

In August, speculation of an imminent rise in the central bank's key lending rate waned as a batch of economic indicators pointed to weakness in the recovery, forcing it to keep an easy credit stance to support the economy.
Economists say the pace of decline in the trade surplus is likely to slow, but even if it started rising again the rise would be very gradual.

"I think we are going to see Japanese exports gaining momentum in the next four to six months. I would expect by the beginning of 1997 that Japanese trade and current account surpluses are going to start to actually grow again very gradually," Koll said.
While encouraging exports, a weak yen was slowing import growth as it made foreign products more expensive in the Japanese market.
The dollar has gained strength against the yen since hitting a record low of 79 yen in April last year. It is now hovering at around 111 yen.
Economists said car exports, which account for a major part of Japan's overall exports, appeared to have bottomed out after earlier declines, and might pick up further this year.
In August, car exports were among items which showed marked increases, along with computers and optical devices. Car exports rose 18.3 percent from a year earlier. ($1=111 yen)
